summary.text: The stratosphere is the second-lowest layer of Earth's atmosphere, lying above the troposphere and below the mesosphere.
Unlike the troposphere below it, it gets warmer with height, because its ozone layer absorbs the Sun's ultraviolet radiation.
Warmer air sitting over cooler air leaves it without regular convection, and in temperate latitudes airliners typically cruise in its lower reaches, above the troposphere's turbulent weather.

facts.label: Lower edge height
facts.value: About 20 km at equator, 7 km at poles

facts.label: Discovered
facts.value: 1902, by Teisserenc de Bort and Assmann

facts.label: Fastest winds
facts.value: Near 60 m/s in the Southern polar vortex

facts.label: Moisture
facts.value: Very dry, because rising air is freeze-dried

items.prompt: You carry a thermometer from the bottom of the stratosphere to its top. What trend do you see?

options.label: It steadily gets colder
It stays the same throughout
It swings up and down randomly
It steadily gets warmer

items.explain: In the stratosphere the warmer layers sit higher and the cooler layers lower, so temperature rises with altitude.

items.prompt: What keeps the upper stratosphere warmer than its lower part?

options.label: Ozone absorbing the Sun's ultraviolet light
Heat rising up from the ground below
Friction from its fast-moving winds
Warm gases from volcanic eruptions

items.explain: Ozone absorbs solar ultraviolet radiation and is broken apart and re-formed over and over, releasing heat and creating the temperature inversion.

items.prompt: Near the ground, warm air rises and stirs things up. Why does air in the stratosphere hardly churn up and down at all?

options.label: The air there is too thin to move
Its strong winds only blow toward the poles
Warmer air sits on top of cooler air
Gravity is much weaker at that height

items.explain: With warmer layers above and cooler ones below, the stratosphere is stable, with no regular convection and the turbulence it brings.

items.prompt: All air entering the stratosphere first passes through the very cold tropopause. What does that do to the air?

options.label: It fills the air with ice clouds
It freeze-dries the air, removing water
It makes the air sink back down
It turns the air's oxygen into ozone

items.explain: Rising air is literally freeze-dried at the tropopause, which is why the stratosphere is a very dry place.

items.prompt: Why do long-distance airliners climb into the lowest part of the stratosphere to cruise?

options.label: The ozone there protects passengers from UV
Air traffic control bans lower flights
Engines need the extra oxygen found there
Cold, thin air cuts drag and saves fuel

items.explain: Low temperatures and low air density near the tropopause reduce drag and optimize fuel efficiency, and the planes stay above the troposphere's turbulent weather.

items.prompt: How does the stratosphere's ozone make life on dry land possible?

options.label: It produces most of the oxygen we breathe
It traps heat to keep the surface warm
It screens out DNA-damaging ultraviolet light
It stops water vapor escaping to space

items.explain: By weakening the solar ultraviolet wavelengths that damage DNA, the ozone layer allows life to exist on the surface outside the ocean.

paragraphs.heading: Second layer up
paragraphs.text: The stratosphere is the second layer of Earth's atmosphere counting from the ground, above the troposphere and beneath the mesosphere. Its name comes from the Ancient Greek word for a layer or stratum. Where it begins depends on where you are: about 20 km up near the equator, around 10 km at mid-latitudes and about 7 km at the poles.

paragraphs.heading: Warmer as you climb
paragraphs.text: In the troposphere below, air cools with height, but the stratosphere gets warmer the higher you go, a reversal called a temperature inversion. The cause is the ozone layer, which absorbs ultraviolet (UV) light from the Sun. Average temperatures run from −51 °C near the tropopause, its lower border, to −15 °C near the mesosphere. The very top, called the stratopause, sits at about 270 K (−3 °C), and above it temperature falls with height.

paragraphs.heading: How ozone heats the air
paragraphs.text: In 1930 the British scientist Sydney Chapman described how the ozone layer forms, a process now called the Chapman cycle. Oxygen molecules (O₂) absorb high-energy UV-C sunlight with wavelengths shorter than about 240 nm and split apart. The freed oxygen atoms join other O₂ molecules to make ozone (O₃). Sunlight breaks ozone much faster than it breaks O₂, giving O and O₂, and the loose atom joins O₂ to rebuild ozone while releasing heat. This rapid breaking and rebuilding is what warms the stratosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Calm, dry and layered
paragraphs.text: With warmer air sitting on cooler air, the stratosphere resists being stirred up and down, which is why it is layered. There is no regular convection here, and none of the turbulence that comes with it. Only very energetic events, such as volcanic eruption columns or the tops of severe thunderstorms, push convection into it, and only briefly and locally. All air entering it must cross the tropopause, a temperature minimum, and is freeze-dried on the way, so the stratosphere is very dry.

paragraphs.heading: Where planes fly
paragraphs.text: Airliners usually cruise at 9 to 12 km, which in temperate latitudes puts them in the lowest part of the stratosphere. The low temperatures and thin air there reduce drag on the airframe and save fuel. Flying this high also keeps them above the turbulent weather of the troposphere. Some aircraft cruised higher still: Concorde flew at Mach 2 at about 18 km, and the SR-71 at Mach 3 at about 26 km.

paragraphs.heading: Winds and circulation
paragraphs.text: Winds here can far outpace those of the troposphere, nearing 60 m/s in the Southern polar vortex. The overall flow is called the Brewer-Dobson circulation, a single loop in which air rises out of the tropical troposphere and sinks outside the tropics. In roughly half of northern hemisphere winters, the stratosphere goes through a sudden warming, caused by the absorption of waves known as Rossby waves.
